text: Japan’s steep climb for modernization also had large detriments environmentally and politically. This is especially noticeable when accounting for Meiji Japan’s imperialistic desires, due to their drive for resources and infrastructure; large-scale deforestation was carried out to fuel factories and railways which in turn caused devastating floods and crop failures (David Fedman, 2020). Most land was redistributed as well, especially arable land, but nationalizing woodlands disrupted traditional land-use. Even politically, Japan gradually regained sovereignty by finally revising unequal treaties in 1894, but it soon became an imperial power itself, following the Western path (Eijiro Honjo, 1932). This was primarily noticeable when Japan engaged in the Sino-Japanese War in 1894-1895 and Russo-Japanese War in 1904-1905 which gave Japan influence over Korea, Taiwan, and parts of China (Columbia Uni., 2025). In short, Japan escaped the grasp of Western rule only to reshape its surroundings by bringing in Japanese customs and bureaucrats into the colonized Korea and Hokkaido regions, which was all at the expense of the indigenous Ainu (Japanese indigenous people).
